δαιμονίζομαι is a denominal -ίζω verb formed on δαίμων, so the supplied possessed answers to no element of it while demons is the root gloss. Rules 66, 91 and 104 head such a unit on the root word — ξενίζω → think it strange on strange, φλογίζω → setteth on fire on fire — as this chapter heads sick of the palsy on palsy at 8:6 and sick of a fever on fever at 8:14. Heading on possessed remains defensible.

A negator standing with a plain indefinite is rule 59's contrast, and that rule joins the pair: the test is whether the second source word is itself a negative — τις is not — and not whether the ASV wrote a single English word, which rule 59 disclaims in terms. no spells the negation and the indefiniteness together, as no-thing does in rule 59's own examples, and man is the generic completion, so rule 17's generic-noun clause holds the target head on no and rule 39's convention puts the source head on the first particle. Splitting no to μή and man to τινά under rule 2, on the model of rule 69's not / any man, remains defensible.

review_notes: Joined μή with the plain indefinite τινά on no man: the accepted split rested on the count of English words, which rule 59 rejects as the test for this construction.
Corrected the head of δαιμονιζόμενοι from possessed to demons, the root gloss of a denominal -ίζω verb (rules 66, 91, 104).
All 30 source and 39 target IDs partitioned exactly once; the ἐκ / ἐξερχόμενοι division follows rule 106's addition clause unchanged.
